title: API server leader lease loss — recovery playbook (WIP)
content:
Background:

This is a working playbook / investigation scratchpad for incidents where the kube-apiserver loses its leader lease (or appears to), producing symptoms across the cluster: elevated pending pods, scheduler backpressure, multiple control-plane components restarting or reporting high latency, and client request timeouts. Historically we've seen this cluster state when etcd I/O stalls, control-plane CPU/GC spikes, or transient network issues between api-servers and etcd leaders.

Scope / goal:
- Provide quick triage checklist for SRE on-call to determine if a leader-lease loss (or perceived lease loss) is the root cause.
- Contain immediate mitigations to restore control-plane responsiveness with minimal blast radius.
- Capture evidence for postmortem and outline follow-ups.

Quick symptoms (what the pager may show):
- Scheduler API calls 5xx / timeout, backlog of pending pods > baseline
- kubectl get nodes / pods slow / hanging
- kube-apiserver logs: "failed to renew lease" or frequent lease acquisition messages
- etcd raft elections spike or high leader-change count
- kube-controller-manager / kube-scheduler restarts or stall messages in logs
- API request latencies for token operations spike (observed in tracing)

Immediate triage (first 10 minutes):
1) Establish scope / blast radius:
   - Which clusters/regions? Check console incident page + slack alerts.
   - How many api-servers are impacted?
2) Check basic health endpoints:
   - kubectl --context CLUSTER-CTX get componentstatuses (may be flaky)
   - kubectl --context CLUSTER-CTX get pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver -o wide
   - kubectl --context CLUSTER-CTX get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -E "etcd|apiserver|scheduler|controller-manager"
3) Inspect api-server logs for lease messages (sample):
   - kubectl logs -n kube-system <kube-apiserver-pod> --tail=200 | grep -i lease
   - Look for lines: "controller-lease lost" / "failed to renew lease" / "time skew"
4) Check etcd health + leadership:
   - kubectl exec -n kube-system etcd-0 -- etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table
   - etcdctl -w table endpoint status --cluster
   - etcdctl endpoint health --cluster
   - etcdctl alarm list
   - Inspect etcd metrics: raft leader changes, commit latency (via our metrics dashboard)
5) Control-plane resource pressure:
   - top/metrics for kube-apiserver CPU/heap/GC latency (from node exporter / process exporter)
   - Node IO/latency if etcd on node-hosted: iostat, dstat
6) Networking check:
   - Are api-servers able to reach etcd endpoints? (tcpdump / curl to client port 2379)
   - Check recent network ACLs / iptables changes / CNI flaps in the past 30m

Common root-cause hypotheses (ordered by frequency seen):
- Etcd leader I/O stall (slow disk/IOPS saturation) -> raft elections -> period without leader
- Etcd compaction/snapshot spike causes CPU/IO bursts on leader -> transient unavailability
- Kube-apiserver GC pause / CPU overload causing missed lease renewals
- Network partition between apiserver and etcd leader (host-level network flaps)
- Time skew on control-plane node(s) causing lease TTL mismatch
- Auto-scaler or autoscaling actions that dramatically changed control-plane capacity simultaneously

Example evidence & how to spot it quickly:
- etcdctl endpoint status shows leader change count increased in last 5m. Metric: etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total
- iostat shows >100ms avg await on etcd nodes for last 10m
- kube-apiserver logs contain repeated "timed out waiting for ..." and GC pause logs (look for "gc controller"?), or very high RSS/heap growth in metrics
- tracer shows control-plane RPCs failing with connection refused or timeout to etcd host

Immediate mitigations (playback; pick the least invasive first):
1) If etcd leader I/O is culprit:
   - Throttle writes from heavy tenants if possible (eg temporarily rate-limit a noisy namespace via admission webhook or api gateway)
   - Move etcd snapshots/compactions off-peak (post-incident), but during incident avoid triggering manual compaction unless instructed by infra lead
   - Consider failing over etcd leadership by restarting the unhealthy etcd member only if you are confident it is the stalled leader and cluster will re-elect quickly (risky)
2) If kube-apiserver CPU/GC is culprit:
   - Rotate api-server pods one at a time (delete pod, let deployment/statefulset recreate) to reclaim memory/clear leaks.
   - If running on static control-plane VMs, consider restarting the apiserver systemd unit on the most overloaded host.
3) Network partition suspicion:
   - Check CNI/node network logs; if only a subset of control-plane replicas can't reach etcd, check host routing and firewall rules.
   - If route/ACL was changed recently, roll back or apply compensating rule.
4) Scheduler backlog mitigation:
   - Temporarily scale up kube-scheduler replicas (if treating it as a deployment) or increase scheduler concurrency settings to drain backlog.
   - As quick bandaid, mark low-priority pods as unschedulable with Taints/Tolerations or suspend a noisy autoscaled job.
5) Avoid mass restarts of etcd unless directed by infra lead. Etcd leader election churn can make things worse if done repeatedly.

Commands (examples) — run with care and context configured:
- etcd status: kubectl exec -n kube-system etcd-0 -- etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table
- leader info: kubectl exec -n kube-system etcd-0 -- etcdctl endpoint status --cluster | grep LEADER
- API server logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system <apiserver> --tail=200 | grep -Ei "lease|renew|failed|timeout|election"
- check raft metrics: query metrics "etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total" in grafana with 1h window
- check scheduler queue: kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -A | wc -l

On-call play-by-play (recommended):
- T+0: Acknowledge + set incident channel. Run quick triage checklist above.
- T+5: If etcd leader churn visible, page infra-engineer (owner: Ravi). Do not restart all members.
- T+10: If API server CPU/GC visible, plan rolling restart of kube-apiserver pods (schedule with prime-time avoidance).
- T+20: If backlog not clearing, scale scheduler(s) / temporarily deprioritize low-priority work.
- T+30: If no improvement, consider controlled failover of etcd leader (infra owner only).

Post-incident followups (owners):
- Runbook cleanup: consolidate evidence steps and automate checks (owner: Asha)
- Dashboard: add a dedicated grafana panel for api-server lease renewal failures + etcd leader changes (owner: Zoe)
- Capacity: validate etcd node disk IOPS and set alerts on high avg await (owner: Miguel)
- SRE automation: add an automated smoke that verifies api-server -> etcd reachability every 5m and raises before pager (owner: Ravi)

Open questions / TODOs:
- How do we reduce blast radius when control-plane autoscaling happens concurrently? Need an inventory of control-plane autoscale triggers.
- Should we add a kube-apiserver healthcheck that includes etcd-specific RPCs (beyond current liveness)? Pros/cons?
- Investigate recent compaction schedule — did we run a manual compaction just before event?

Notes to self (handy lines):
- Don’t run etcdctl member remove unless instructed by infra owner and after backups.
- Capture logs from all apiserver replicas (not just leader) for the 30m window: use kubectl logs --since=30m on each
- If you see time skew >1s between control-plane hosts, coordinate NTP fix prior to cluster-facing changes.

Annex — sample log excerpts to look for:
- "E1123 12:03:21.123456 1 lease.go:xxx] failed to renew lease: context deadline exceeded"
- "2019-11-23 12:03:22.123456 I | raft: leader changed: from 2 to 1"
- "etcdserver: request timed out"

Last incident note (for context):
- On 2024-08-28 cluster-prod-3 had intermittent apiserver timeouts due to heavy compaction on etcd leader; root cause was snapshot schedule overlapping with a crash-looping job that increased writes. Mitigations then were: throttle job, bump etcd nodes to faster disk type, and reschedule compaction window.

If you're reading this during an incident: start the checklist, call out infra-owner early, and log decisions in the incident channel. Keep restarts minimal and prefer rolling operations.

-- end of WIP playbook --
